Properties linked to money laundering case lift auction sales value in 3Q2026
article:
The auction market saw 163 listings during the third quarter of this year, including 26 linked to Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case, according to a Knight Frank Singapore research report published on Oct 26.

In late August, Deloitte Singapore — which is handling the liquidation of non-cash assets seized in the case —  said over 80 real estate properties would be among assets auctioned in phases between September 2026 and mid-2027.

Of the 26 seized properties listed for auction in 3Q2026, four were successfully sold under the hammer.

They comprise two units at Modern Modern, a condo in River Valley, and two units at Wallich Residence , the residential component of Guoco Tower in Tanjong Pagar. Both are 99-year leasehold projects.

The Martin Modern units were both two-bedders that fetched $2.12 million and $2.08 million, while the Wallich Residence units comprised four-bedders that sold for $6.6 million and $5.48 million.

All four properties were sold below their respective opening bid prices.

Together, the properties fetched a combined sales value of $16.3 million. This accounted for  two-thirds of the auction market’s total gross sales value of $24.1 million across nine properties sold in 3Q2026.

Based on the 163 total listings in the third quarter, the nine properties sold translates to an auction success rate of 5.5%,  similar to the 5.7% rate garnered in 2Q2026.

“The high-profile listings have drawn greater attention to property auctions, but buyers remain selective,” said Nicholas Keong, Knight Frank’s head of auction, residential and private office.

Auction listings in the third quarter included 77 mortgagee sales and 41 owner's sales. The remaining 45 included the properties seized in the money laundering case as well as other auction sale types (MCST, sheriff, estate and public trustee sales).

The 77 mortgagee sale listings represent a 29.4% decline from the quarter before. They comprised 38 residences, 29 industrial properties, nine retail shops and one office unit.

Two of the residences were sold through auction: a three-bedder at Ava Towers , a freehold condo off Balestier Road in District 12, and a two-bedder at Hilltops , a freehold condo on Cairnhill Circle in District 9.

Owner listings, which rose 28.1% q-o-q from the 32 listings in 2Q2026, were largely made up of residences (30), followed by industrial (9) and retail (2) properties.

Only one owner's sale listing was sold in the third quarter: a freehold one-bedroom unit at residential development Suites @Braddell that fetched $636,600, 1.3% above its opening price.

Two properties that were auctioned successfully were MCST sales. They consisted of a three-bedroom unit at Orchid Park Condominium in Yishun and a ramp-up warehouse unit at The Westcom , a Business 2 industrial development in Tuas.

Knight Frank's Keong expects the auction market to “remain stable” through the rest of the year, supported by “a steady stream of mortgagee and owner sales”.

Despite heightened interest from the introduction of properties linked to the money laundering case, auction bidding activity and prices achieved continue to rely on buyers’ assessment of  “the fundamental values of these properties based on their individual characteristics”, he added.

title: Park Hyatt Phu Quoc to debut in December; Fusion opens Legacy Hanoi
article:
Vietnam's hospitality scene will see two more properties debuting this year — Park Hyatt is set to open its first resort in the country on Phu Quoc island in December 2026, while Fusion Hotel Group has launched its 218-room Legacy Hanoi in September.

Park Hyatt Phu Quoc

Park Hyatt Phu Quoc will occupy a 65ha site along 1.7km of white-sand beach on the island's southwest coast.

Inspired by traditional Vietnamese coastal villages, the resort is arranged around courtyards, shaded pathways and gardens leading towards the sea.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

Accommodation will comprise 114 guestrooms and suites, 54 pool villas, as well as The Manor — an eight-bedroom private residence designed for multigenerational stays.

At the centre of the resort, The Courtyard will house six dining venues, two ocean-facing infinity pools and a sunset bar.

Dining options include Fisherman's, a floating restaurant where guests can select seafood from a live tank, and Pepper Grill, which draws on Phu Quoc's pepper-growing heritage.

The resort will also introduce Soma Wellbeing, Park Hyatt's first spa organised around circadian rhythms. Located beside a lotus lake, it will offer traditional Vietnamese treatments alongside recovery facilities such as infrared masks and compression therapy.

Other activities include visits to local pepper farms and fish sauce producers, fishing experiences and guided activities at the island's rice paddies. A Kids' Village will offer culinary classes, dance and craft workshops.

Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is approximately 25 minutes by car from Phu Quoc International Airport, which has direct flights from Singapore and several other Asian cities.

Legacy Hanoi

Fusion Hotel Group held the grand opening of Legacy Hanoi on Sept 16, marking its debut in Vietnam's capital.

Located in the historic Ngoc Ha ward, the property comprises 85 hotel rooms and 133 serviced apartments. Accommodation ranges from studios to one- and two-bedroom units, measuring between 37 sq m (398 sq ft) and 105 sq m (1,130 sq ft).

The hotel rooms occupy floors 14 to 18, while the serviced apartments are located on floors 9 to 13 and 19 to 21.

Hotel rooms and suites feature private balconies, floor-to-ceiling windows and vintage record players. The apartments have wooden finishes with indigo blue and terracotta accents.

The interiors draw on Hanoi's heritage, with references to the historic O Quan Chuong Gate, the Red River and the five-petal peach blossom. A suspended sculpture inspired by the Vietnamese crane, or chim hac, hangs above the reception area.

On the 24th floor, Moc Loft serves contemporary interpretations of Northern Vietnamese dishes, while 24 Social and Terrace offers an open-air rooftop bar overlooking the city.

The hotel's Yen Spa, meanwhile, offers Vietnamese massage and beauty treatments, alongside an onsen facility with hot and cold pools, a sauna, steam room and relaxation lounge.

title: Higher demand for terraced homes as some buyers priced out of semi-detached segment: Huttons
article:
Semi-detached homes saw the biggest price jump among landed housing segments in the last quarter, despite lower sales volume.

Excluding Good Class Bungalows (GCBs) and strata landed homes, prices of landed houses grew by 3.7% q-o-q in 3Q2026 to an average of $2,275 psf, URA data compiled by Huttons Data Analytics showed.

Overall volume and average price of landed homes

While all landed home segments saw price increases, the semi-detached segment recorded the biggest growth, rising 4.7% from an average of $1,989 psf in 2Q2026 to $2,082 psf during the last quarter.

Prices of terraced homes rose 2.7% q-o-q to $2,400 psf across the same period, while those for detached homes grew 1.4% to $2,046 psf.

This comes despite fewer semi-detached homes transacted. The segment saw 143 units sold in 3Q2026, falling 13.3% q-o-q. In contrast, terraced home sales remained steady in the last quarter — at 300 units, on a par with the 301 sold in 2Q2026.

Detached homes saw a slight decrease in sales volume, going from 50 units in 2Q2026 to 44 units in the last quarter.

“As some buyers were priced out of the semi-detached market, demand shifted towards terraced homes,” Huttons stated in its latest quarterly report on the landed market, published on Oct 26.

Transaction volume and average prices of landed homes by segment

In absolute terms, semi-detached homes were transacted at an average of $6.9 million in 3Q2026, rising 4.2% q-o-q. In comparison, prices of terraced and detached homes declined by 1.9% and 4.9% to $4.7 million and $13.0 million, respectively.

Overall, a total of 487 landed housing transactions were recorded in 3Q2023, excluding GCBs and strata landed homes. This is 5.6% less than the 516 deals logged in the previous quarter.

Huttons attributed the fall to seasonal factors that included the Lunar Seventh Month, along with slower activity in the HDB and private condo resale markets.

It added that rising land costs were prompting more buyers to opt for smaller landed properties. “The average land size of transacted landed homes shrank from 3,079 sq ft in 2Q2026 to 2,910 sq ft in 3Q2026,” the report stated.

In addition to smaller plots, landed homebuyers were also turning to shorter tenures, noted Lee Sze Teck, Huttons’ senior director of data analytics.

This comes amid a broadening price gap between freehold and 999-year leasehold homes compared to those with 99-year tenures.

“The price gap between 999-year leasehold/freehold and 99-year leasehold landed homes in 3Q2026 widened to 51.2%, the biggest since 2020,” he said.

As a result, there was a slightly higher proportion of 99-year leasehold landed transactions in the last quarter. These homes accounted for 15.6% of all landed housing deals in 3Q2026, up by 2.4 percentage points and the highest since 1Q2025.

Looking ahead, landed property volumes may “dip slightly” in 4Q2026 due to the year-end holidays, Lee noted. Nonetheless, backed by persistent demand, their prices should “stay firm”.

title: URA awards Marina Gardens Lane GLS site to EL Development at $1,243 psf ppr
article:
URA has awarded the tender for a Government Land Sale (GLS) site at Marina Gardens Lane to EL Development for $450.1 million, or $1,243 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr).

The tender for the residential site with ground-floor commercial space closed on Oct 15, with EL Development the sole bidder.

The developer’s offer fell below analysts' expectations of three to six bids and a top bid between $1,350 and $1,650 psf ppr.

The land rate is 11.3% lower than the $1,402 psf ppr Kingsford Group paid in 2023 for a neighbouring plot, which is now the site of the 937-unit One Marina Gardens .

However, it is higher than the $984 psf ppr offer URA rejected in 2024 for a nearby GLS site at Marina Gardens Crescent. The sole bid by GuocoLand, Hong Leong Holdings and TID for the white site was deemed to be too low.

The Marina Gardens Lane plot awarded to EL Development measures 64,659 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 362,119 sq ft. The 99-year leasehold site can yield about 390 homes and up to 1,615 sq ft of first-floor commercial space.

Based on the $1,243 psf ppr land rate, analysts predict future homes on the site could launch at average prices ranging from $2,500 to around $2,900 psf.

title: Shangri-La Singapore unveils refurbished Valley Wing with two Presidential Suites
article:
Shangri-La Singapore has unveiled its refurbished Valley Wing, with redesigned guest rooms and suites, including two Presidential Suites.

The luxury hotel’s refurbishment covered the Valley Wing's Executive Rooms, Executive Suites, Premier Suites and two Presidential Suites: the Shangri-La Suite and Singapore Suite.

Located within Shangri-La Singapore's 15-acre (6.07ha) grounds along Orange Grove Road, near Orchard Road, the Valley Wing has its own private driveway, lobby and check-in area, separate from the hotel's other accommodation wings.

Interiors inspired by Singapore's heritage

The redesigned interiors draw inspiration from Singapore's historic shophouses and tropical landscape, combining Asian decorative elements with European classical influences.

Geometric latticework, architectural mouldings and decorative panels reference traditional shophouse architecture.

Botanical wallpaper depicting tropical foliage, flowering branches and wildlife complements the soft greens, muted golds and warm neutrals used throughout the rooms and suites.

The Executive Rooms feature updated furnishings and seating areas, while the larger Executive and Premier Suites provide additional living space.

Two refurbished Presidential Suites

The largest accommodation in the hotel is the 348 sq m (3,746 sq ft) Shangri-La Suite, which has separate living and dining areas for private gatherings and entertaining.

The suite includes an upgraded 85-inch television, a private gym, its own lift and dedicated 24-hour butler service.

The second Presidential Suite, named the Singapore Suite, has two bedrooms, spacious living areas, panoramic views and a private whirlpool bath.

Both suites feature wall murals depicting tropical landscapes and floral designs, as well as upholstered furnishings and warm-toned interiors.

Exclusive facilities for Valley Wing guests

The Valley Wing retains its dedicated guest facilities, including the Summit Room, where breakfast is served, and the Valley Wing Lounge.

Guests can enjoy afternoon tea, champagne and refreshments at the lounge throughout the day, followed by evening cocktails and canapés.

“With this transformation, our vision was to honour the timeless elegance and sense of exclusivity that guests have come to cherish, while introducing a renewed expression of luxury that feels both contemporary and deeply connected to Singapore's heritage,” says Stephan Kapek, vice-president of operations and general manager of Shangri-La Singapore.

title: YZJ MARITIME: Why Chairman Ren Yuanlin Is Bullish About Next 8–10 Years
article:
Yangzijiang Maritime Development's 1H 2026 results presented a contrast: business is expanding rapidly, but profits are moving in the opposite direction.

Total income jumped
49% to US$81.6 million
, driven by a 70% surge in maritime income to US$51.7 million. Yet net profit attributable to shareholders fell 29% to US$44.9 million.

So when will this expansion pay off? Executive chairman
Ren Yuanlin
offered an answer at a 14 Oct Phillip Securities webinar: from 2027 through 2030.

A property developer — for ships

As background, Y

angzijiang Maritime Development traces its roots to
Yangzijiang Shipbuilding
, which listed on the SGX in 2007 and built up a substantial investment business.
In April 2022, Yangzijiang Shipbuilding spun off its investment arm as
Yangzijiang Financial Holding
.
Yangzijiang Financial subsequently expanded into maritime investments, including vessel financing, leasing and shipbuilding projects.
In November 2025, it spun off these maritime businesses into
Yangzijiang Maritime Development.
Listed on the SGX on 18 Nov 2025, Yangzijiang Maritime became the third listed company in the Yangzijiang family, led by veteran shipbuilder
Ren Yuanlin
.

An easy way to understand Yangzijiang Maritime is to think of a property developer, but for ships.
It arranges for vessels to be built at favourable prices, then sells them, sometimes before completion, or charters them out for recurring income.

The company works with second- and third-tier Chinese shipyards that have spare capacity but may struggle to attract international customers or secure refund guarantees.
Yangzijiang Maritime contributes technical expertise, vessel designs and procurement know-how.

Management says this combination can deliver building costs
up to 20% below prevailing first-tier shipyard prices
.

Ren said vessel sales typically earn profit margins of 15–20%, although construction takes two to three years. Importantly, that is not the same as a 15–20% annual return or group net profit margin.

A case study in the company's presentation illustrates the attraction: two vessels were sold before completion, generating more than US$20 million in combined profit.

Bullish assessment from industry veteran

Yangzijiang Maritime chairman Ren Yuanlin expressed confidence that the shipping and shipbuilding industry could enjoy another 8–10 years of strong business conditions, despite the weakness in China's economy and the broader global economy.

Drawing on his more than 50 years of industry experience, he gave three main reasons:

1.
Strong demand to replace ageing ships
. The need to replace ageing vessels will keep shipyards busy for years.
With many major shipyards already heavily booked, he sees limited capacity to accommodate additional demand, supporting a prolonged industry upcycle.

2.
Growing energy demand from AI.
Ren argued that AI's enormous electricity requirements would increase demand for energy, including oil and gas.
Transporting these commodities would support demand for tankers and other vessels.

3.
Geopolitical tensions are increasing shipping demand
. Conflicts and disruptions force vessels to take longer routes to avoid dangerous areas.
Consequently, ships take longer to complete voyages, reducing effective fleet capacity and supporting demand for additional vessels.

U

S$500 million of vessel sales

By August, Yangzijiang Maritime had signed 12 vessel sale contracts worth an aggregate
US$500 million
. Four involved newbuild bulk carriers. The US$500 million is gross contract value.

At the webinar, management outlined expected deliveries of nine vessels in 2026, 16–18 in 2027 and 24–26 in 2028, with the remaining pipeline extending into 2029–2030.

More deliveries should mean more opportunities for vessel sales and charter income. But they also create commitments to fund construction.

Why the profit squeeze?

Management acknowledged that the expanding business has pushed operating costs higher. It has also been moving vessels from time charters to spot charters to capture potentially higher freight rates.
Bringing charter vessels into operation can involve one-off startup costs of several hundred thousand US dollars per ship. Spot exposure may increase revenue in favourable markets, but also adds volatility.
And there was a major contributor: FX losses.
The swing in currency-related gains and losses was US$21.7 million, exceeding the US$18.6 million decline in reported net profit. DBS consequently estimated that profit excluding the FX effects actually rose about 7% year on year.

Bringing charter vessels into operation can involve one-off startup costs of several hundred thousand US dollars per ship. Spot exposure may increase revenue in favourable markets, but also adds volatility.

To share risks, Yangzijiang Maritime co-invests with established European ship operators, which commonly take equity stakes of 10–30%.
If resale prices are unattractive when vessels are completed, those partners can operate the ships to earn charter income instead.

A

Hong Kong possibility

Ren reiterated the company's guideline to distribute
40% of net profit as dividends
.

The company's balance sheet provides some reassurance.
At end-June, it had US$238 million in cash and net assets of approximately S$2.3 billion, equivalent to
60.87 Singapore cents per share
.

Ren also disclosed that management is exploring Hong Kong depositary receipts, which would allow investors in Hong Kong to trade an interest in Yangzijiang Maritime's shares without buying the shares directly on the SGX.  Nothing definite has been announced.

For shareholders, the central question is not how many ships Yangzijiang Maritime can order. It is how profitably — and how quickly — those ships can be monetised.

Ren expects a richer harvest from 2027. The challenge now is to turn the expanding vessel portfolio into higher profits and cash flow — and demonstrate that shareholders' patience is justified.

title: SGX Next 50: Top 3 REITs to Watch This Week
article:

Keppel REIT: Will a bigger portfolio start paying more per unit?
Keppel REIT owns 14 prime commercial assets across Singapore, Australia, South Korea and Japan, with assets under management (AUM) of S$11.8 billion as at 30 June 2026.
Keppel REIT’s purchases lifted its first-half 2026 (1H2026) numbers.
It bought a 75% interest in Top Ryde City Shopping Centre in December 2025 and took a further one-third stake in Marina Bay Financial Centre Tower 3.
Property income rose 16.7% year on year (YoY) to S$159.3 million, while distributable income expanded 22.8% to S$129.6 million.
Unitholders did not see the benefit.
Distribution per unit (DPU) fell 4.0% YoY to S$0.0261 because an enlarged unit base diluted the gains.
In other words, the pie grew, but each slice got smaller.
The buildings themselves remain well let.
Committed portfolio occupancy stood at a healthy 96.0%, accompanied by a positive rental reversion of 12.8%, meaning new and renewed leases were signed at higher rental rates.
North Asia is the soft patch.
Attributable net property income (NPI) from the region fell 12.0%YoY, while Singapore and Australia grew 23.5% and 21.2%, respectively.
So what should you watch on 28 October?
Start with KR Ginza II.
The manager previously agreed to sell the Tokyo building for JPY 11.52 billion (28.4% above its 2022 purchase cost), with completion expected in the third quarter of 2026.
Check whether it has closed.
If the REIT pays out any gain, keep that sum separate from ordinary DPU.
On debt, aggregate leverage stood at 40.0%, with a weighted average cost of debt of 3.27% per annum.

Starhill Global REIT: Can new luxury tenants restart Wisma Atria’s sales?
Starhill Global REIT, or SGREIT, owns nine predominantly retail properties across six Asia-Pacific cities, with a total portfolio valuation of around S$2.7 billion as at 30 June 2026.
SGREIT is the quiet one of the trio.
For its fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2025/2026), NPI rose 0.1% YoY to S$150.3 million, while DPU rose 0.8% to S$0.0368.
Committed portfolio occupancy improved to 97.2% from 94.6% a year earlier.
Gearing stood at 35.8%, with around 80% of debt on fixed or hedged rates.
Wisma Atria is the property to watch.
Tenant sales there fell 3.7% YoY, which the manager attributed to downtime at the Level 2 façade units ahead of new luxury tenants.
Watch whether those tenants have opened and sales have turned.
Currency is another swing factor.
A stronger ringgit and Australian dollar helped lift SGREIT’s FY2025/2026 results.
A reversal would work against the REIT.
SGREIT also did not disclose rental reversion last period, so any update would reveal its pricing power.

Lendlease Global Commercial REIT: How much growth is left once PLQ Mall is in the base?
Lendlease Global Commercial REIT, or LREIT, owns Jem, 313@somerset and PLQ Mall in Singapore, plus three Grade A commercial buildings in Milan.
LREIT sold Jem’s office component and bought PLQ Mall in two tranches, completed in November 2025 and March 2026.
For the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), NPI rose 2.7% YoY to S$152.7 million.
Distributable income jumped 26.0% to S$110.3 million, aided by lower interest expenses and reduced perpetual securities distributions.
Full-year DPU grew at a more modest 3.0% to S$0.037.
PLQ Mall flatters the headline numbers.
Shopper traffic grew 16.4% YoY and tenant sales rose 24.0% across LREIT’s Singapore retail portfolio.
Strip out PLQ Mall, and those increases shrink to 5.2% and 4.0%.
Those are the numbers to track.
LREIT’s committed occupancy slipped to 94.6% from 95.3% a quarter earlier.
Retail occupancy stood at 98.5%, while office occupancy lagged at 89.1%.
On a positive note, LREIT has strengthened its balance sheet.
Gearing fell to 38.9% from 42.6% a year earlier, and the cost of debt dropped to 2.75% per annum.
Watch, too, for news on the 313@somerset event space, due in the second half of 2026.
Get Smart: Follow the growth down to your units
When a REIT grows through
acquisitions
, compare its distributable income growth with its DPU growth.
The gap tells you how much of that expansion you actually own.
Keppel REIT and LREIT both opened up a wide gap in their latest reporting periods.
SGREIT’s NPI barely grew, yet its DPU still rose.
So when these three report later this week, ask each one the same question: is the growth finally reaching your units?

title: Want S$3,000 a Month in Retirement? Here’s How CPF LIFE and Dividend Stocks Can Work Together

You want S$3,000 a month in retirement.
You start doing the maths.
At a 4% dividend yield, you’ll need S$900,000 invested to generate that income.
That’s when retirement starts to feel rather expensive.
But what if you don’t actually need S$900,000?
What if part of your retirement income is already taken care of?
That’s where CPF LIFE comes in.
By combining CPF LIFE payouts with dividends from Singapore stocks and real estate investment trusts (REITs), you could reduce the amount your investment portfolio needs to generate.
And as we’ll see, the difference could be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.
How Much Can CPF LIFE Pay You Every Month?
CPF LIFE provides monthly payouts for as long as you live, helping Singaporeans manage the risk of outliving their retirement savings.
How much CPF LIFE pays you depends on your Retirement Account savings, the plan you choose and when you start receiving payouts.
CPF has three retirement sum reference levels: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), Full Retirement Sum (FRS) and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS).

CPF LIFE vs Dividend Stocks: What’s the Difference?
CPF LIFE and
dividend stocks
can complement each other, but they serve different purposes.
CPF LIFE provides lifelong monthly payouts, while dividend stocks offer the potential for additional income and capital appreciation.
There are important differences in how much flexibility and certainty each provides.

For instance, CPF LIFE could help cover essential household expenses, while dividend income provides additional flexibility for discretionary spending.
The aim isn’t necessarily to choose one over the other, but to understand what each can contribute to your retirement income plan.
Should You Put More Money Into CPF or Dividend Stocks?
This is where
retirement income planning
becomes more personal.
Additional CPF retirement savings can increase your eventual lifelong payouts. CPF LIFE also offers an Escalating Plan, which starts with lower payouts that increase over time.
However, CPF savings are subject to withdrawal restrictions.
Dividend investments offer greater flexibility because you can generally sell your shares when you need access to capital, although doing so during a downturn could mean accepting losses.
Consider two investors targeting S$3,000 monthly.
One might prefer to build up CPF savings for higher lifelong payouts. Another might prioritise an accessible investment portfolio, accepting the possibility of fluctuating dividends and share prices.
The appropriate balance depends on your existing CPF savings, retirement timeline, liquidity needs and willingness to take investment risks.
Don’t Let a High Dividend Yield Fool You
Remember our earlier calculation?
To generate S$14,640 annually, you would need S$366,000 invested at a 4% dividend yield.
At 6%, you would need just S$244,000.
That’s S$122,000 less investment capital.
Tempting, isn’t it?
But there’s a reason investors shouldn’t chase the
highest dividend yield
.
A yield can rise simply because a company’s share price has fallen. If earnings weaken or debt becomes harder to manage, that attractive yield may not last.
For investors building retirement income from Singapore dividend stocks and REITs, three questions matter:
Can the business sustain its dividends?
Examine earnings, cash flow, debt and payout commitments.
Is your income diversified?
Relying heavily on a few banks or REITs could expose your portfolio to sector-specific problems.
Can you manage uneven payouts?
Dividends may arrive quarterly or half-yearly, so cash reserves can help cover monthly spending.
A sustainable 4% yield may ultimately serve your retirement needs better than a 6% yield that gets cut, although neither outcome is guaranteed.
How to Build Your S$3,000 Monthly Retirement Income Plan
Start by estimating your monthly retirement expenses, then check how much CPF LIFE could provide using CPF Board’s
Retirement Payout Planner
.
Next, calculate your remaining income gap and assess whether your investment portfolio can realistically generate the difference.
Finally, consider whether your investments are sufficiently diversified and whether their income can remain sustainable through different market conditions.
Reaching S$3,000 a month in retirement isn’t necessarily about accumulating a S$900,000 dividend portfolio.
Depending on your CPF LIFE payouts, the amount your investments need to generate could be considerably smaller.
The challenge is building that additional income without taking unnecessary risks simply to chase higher yields.
A good retirement plan isn’t about making every dollar work harder. It’s about making sure each source of income has a job to do.

title: US stocks gain as investors parse Anthropic IPO filing
article:
(Oct 26): US stocks gained on Monday as investors digest Anthropic PBC’s filing for its initial public offering (IPO) and look forward to key big tech earnings this week as well as the Federal Reserve’s next decision on Wednesday.

The S&P 500 Index gained 0.9% as of 11.31am in New York, while the Nasdaq 100 was up 1.4%. Brent crude fell 0.42% to US$116 a barrel.

“With so many firms reporting this week, we would typically say that macro factors will take a back seat to idiosyncratic results. However, we have the Fed on Wednesday and what could be a very tricky, complicated press conference,” wrote Christopher Harvey, head of equity and portfolio strategy at CIBC, in a note. “We think Wednesday afternoon will be all about the macro, but by roughly 4.30pm that day, GOOGL and MSFT will take centre stage, and earnings are expected to trump the Fed.”

Anthropic filed its much-awaited S-1, moving a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models to go public. Investors are parsing through all of the facts and figures, with an emphasis on what they mean for AI demand after weeks of doubt in the market.

In addition, Meta Platforms Inc said it is aiming to raise as much as US$95 billion from the sale of common and preferred stock to fund AI spending, and SpaceX signed a roughly US$40 billion equipment-finance lease with Apollo Global Management Inc to pay for the chips needed to fuel its AI ambitions.

See also: CoreWeave rout sends warning sign to rest of stock market

Focus on Monday will also be on the impact from President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s runoff election against market favourite Flávio Bolsonaro. US-listed shares of Brazilian companies and those exposed to the country slumped, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF tumbled 21%.

Last week was a roller coaster ride for the stock market, with the Nasdaq falling 2.9% on Thursday, a day after Meta raised its capex guidance to above its operating cash flow, spooking investors looking for evidence that massive spending on AI is paying off. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, or SOX, tumbled 6.7% on Thursday, while investors rotated into defensive sectors.

Concerns are spilling into credit, with the price of five-year credit default swaps on Meta’s debt recently spiking to a record high. And on Sunday, Elon Musk wrote in a post on X that “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres.”

See also: Growth, value stocks set for reshuffle as S&P adopts new rules

This week will bring more tech results to review, with Alphabet Inc and Microsoft Corp set to report on Wednesday, and Amazon.com Inc and Intel Corp reporting on Thursday. Amid the big tech earnings, investors are also awaiting the Federal Reserve’s meeting on Wednesday, where policymakers are anticipated to leave rates unchanged after raising them in September.

The jitters throughout the market have been enough to turn Max Kettner, chief multi-asset strategist at HSBC, cautious on stocks. The long-time equity bull tactically cut his maximum overweight in stocks to neutral on AI regulation fears heading into the Midterm elections.

In single stock moves, Tesla rose 6.2% as Barclays joins peers on upgrading the electric-car maker, citing M&A opportunity with SpaceX.

title: Bitcoin dips below US$80,000 as AI-related market selloff deepens
article:
(Oct 26): Bitcoin retreated below US$80,000 on as investors remained cautious while weathering big swings in tech earnings for clues on the outlook for the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

The largest digital asset fell as much as 1.4% to under US$79,280 on Monday. Smaller tokens including Ether, XRP and Solana also declined. The moves came after investors pulled US$772.4 million from US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Thursday and Friday, a sharp reversal from more than US$1 billion of net inflows earlier in the week.

“Whenever there’s fear due to macro related events that affect equities it often ends up trickling down to crypto as well.” said Martin Lee, content and market insights lead at DWF Labs. “But BTC has been holding up relatively well, dipping lesser than the Nasdaq two weeks ago and only slightly more last week.”

Bitcoin remains in the risk-off basket for many systematic funds and algorithmic traders, leaving it vulnerable to deteriorating sentiment, said Pratik Kala, portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto.

Another major support for the original cryptocurrency has weakened. The largest Bitcoin accumulator, Strategy Inc, paused token purchases for the first time in five weeks. The firm has been one of the biggest buyers this year, buying billions of dollars of the digital asset by raising funds through the sale of common and preferred stock.

See also: Bitcoin falls below US$83,000 as AI jitters weigh on sentiment

Shares of Strategy dropped around 3.7%. The stocks of other crypto-related companies also declined, with Coinbase Global Inc falling 2.6% and Circle Internet Group Inc slumping 6.8%.

“Bitcoin has so far been relatively resilient to the AI debt concerns that are weighing on all risk assets,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. “The market focus is now on the Fed meeting, followed by US midterm elections.”

Kala pointed to online discussions about AI, including comments from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk about potential consolidation next year, as contributing to market strain. Advances in AI have also exacerbated potential security risks for crypto, making some investors skittish, he added.

title: CoreWeave rout sends warning sign to rest of stock market
article:
(Oct 26): Wall Street strategists are warning that declines in shares of artificial intelligence (AI) cloud-computing providers will spill into other corners of the tech trade, potentially dragging the US stock market down to its June lows.

CoreWeave Inc, the company at the centre of the tumult after its bonds plunged to distressed levels this month, saw its shares drop 41% since Oct 6 as of Friday’s close, when major US equity indices hit a fresh record. Shares of other neoclouds — companies that provide computing power to firms building and running AI models — have also posted double-digit declines during that time. Iren Ltd is down 40% while Nebius Group NV has dropped 36%.

Investors are concerned about the amount of debt companies involved in the AI build-out have borrowed and are worried about how much more they’ll take on after reporting earnings. These fears pushed measures of credit risk for some of the biggest technology companies spending on AI developments to new highs last week.

After a bruising Thursday during which the Nasdaq 100 declined nearly 3% and the S&P 500 had its worst day since late July, strategists see the impact on the equity market deepening.

“It’s now transitioning from being a micro event to a macro event,” Brian Reynolds, chief market strategist at Reynolds Strategy LLC, said of the selloff in neoclouds. “In other words, it’s not just impacting the neoclouds, but the entire credit market and then the stock market.”

Reynolds expects additional selling that could push the S&P 500 back down to its lows of early June. That would mean a 4.7% drop from where the benchmark closed on Friday.

See also: US stocks gain as investors parse Anthropic IPO filing

Neoclouds are massively reliant on issuing bonds to fund their spending. But with US Treasury yields climbing and inflation remaining entrenched, the cost of financing is rising. Ohsung Kwon, chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo & Co, said that if neoclouds cut future capital expenditure plans to assuage investor concerns, that would be a major headwind to semiconductors, whose revenue comes directly from data-centre developers paying huge sums of money for chips.

“If they start to see risk around their financing and the market pushes back on their capex a lot more than what we’re seeing today, and if they cut capex next year, that’s going to be a risk to semis,” Kwon said in an interview.

See also: Growth, value stocks set for reshuffle as S&P adopts new rules

Those fears could come to reality, with Elon Musk warning that the “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres.”

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote in a post on X on Sunday, referring to guppy fish, which can go in to shock during a change in environment. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Concerns over neocloud woes have weighed on the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index, which has dropped more than 13% so far in October.

More than just tech, multiple Wall Street strategists have now warned the meltdown in neoclouds is offering the broader market a reality check at a time when investors are anxious about an AI bubble.

“If the AI bubble is going to burst, it’ll likely start as a credit event as neocloud and risky AI debt defaults, creating a cascade of devaluations, reduced spending and contraction [in multiples and growth],” Sevens Report founder Tom Essaye wrote in a note last week. He added that he’s continuing to watch for signs of stress in the credit markets.

Neocloud stocks are currently showing “asymmetric” responses to credit stresses, according to Barclays plc strategists led by Venu Krishna.

“Widening spreads prompt outsized declines, while tightening provides limited relief, underscoring skepticism around the neocloud business model’s durability,” they wrote in a note last week.

While Krishna said he was looking for “signs of contagion” in the equity market, he’s not seeing evidence the issue has spread beyond tech and growth stocks just yet. Investors have been rotating out of high-flying technology stocks and into defensive sectors, signalling uncertainty around the AI trade rather than indiscriminate selling when everything gets hit simultaneously.

Still, selling in the market’s largest sector by weight has dragged indices lower. On Thursday, for example, the S&P 500 fell more than 1% even though it had more gainers than decliners.

Reynolds said the US benchmark, which broke below its 50-day moving average on Thursday, may fall all the way to its June lows, at which point he would be a buyer.

“I want to be defensive in the very near term, for a few weeks,” Reynolds said. “I really want to buy at that low 7,200 area.”

title: Apple debuts US$699 water-resistant iPad mini with OLED screen
article:
(Oct 26): Apple Inc on Monday unveiled a revamped iPad mini with an OLED display, water-resistant design and faster chip, kicking off a week of product launches.

The tablet, priced at US$699, features an 8.5-inch OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, screen that delivers deeper blacks, brighter whites and improved contrast. Apple has increased the display size from the previous 8.3 inches by slimming down the bezels around the panel. The redesigned device also includes a new “Acoustic Display” audio system that places the speakers beneath the display, helping to make this the first iPad with an IP67 dust and water resistance rating.

The new iPad mini is 14% thinner and 13% lighter than its predecessor, and Apple has repositioned the front-facing camera so that it’s better suited for FaceTime calls and video conferencing.

Inside, it features the A20 Pro chip, an upgrade from the A17 Pro processor in the previous iPad mini, which started at US$599. It’s being offered with standard and matte nano-texture display options and storage configurations ranging from 128 gigabytes (GB) to 512GB. Fully outfitted with the maximum amount of storage, an etched matte screen and cellular connectivity, the tablet can cost as much as US$1,249.

Apple has also upgraded the new model with its N1 networking chip, bringing WiFi 7 and Bluetooth 6 to the iPad mini. Cellular models are equipped with the company’s C2 modem.

The latest iPad mini kicks off a series of late-October product introductions from Apple. Later this week, the company plans to unveil a new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, before closing out the week with its first touch-screen MacBook Pro.

See also: Apple's iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply, high demand

Pre-orders for the new iPad mini begin on Wednesday and it goes on sale on Nov 6. The latest model comes in “midnight” and “starlight” colour options.

The A20 Pro chip on the iPad mini is being offered in two versions: The 128GB and 256GB models include five CPU, or main processing cores, while the higher-end configuration has six cores. Both use seven graphics cores. The higher-end variant also has a dual 16-core Neural Engine for enhanced artificial intelligence processing.

Apple is holding a launch event on Wednesday in Los Angeles, where members of the press and content creators will get hands-on time with the new devices. The introductions cap a busy year of product releases for Apple, including last Friday’s launch of the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone.

See also: UK said to push for carve-out from new EU tech sovereignty rules

Bloomberg News first reported on the new iPad mini last year. The company is also working on a new low-end iPad, OLED iPad Air and refreshed iPad Pro for the first half of next year.

title: Anthropic flags ‘existential risks’ in long-awaited IPO filing
article:
(Oct 26): Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering (IPO), warning its technology carried existential risks even as it moved a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models to go public.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing on Monday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

The IPO is being led Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley, along with 20 other banks, the filing showed. Anthropic and some of its shareholders are offering stock in the IPO, according to the filing. The amount of shares they are offering will be disclosed in a later filing.

The company’s debut has become a focal point for the world’s hopes and fears over AI, which run the gamut from worries over job displacement and the substantial upfront spending the technology needs to other, more existential questions: Anthropic’s prospectus has flagged various “risks to humanity” including attempts to “resist shutdown” and “conceal or manipulate information”.

Anthropic had an US$80.7 billion ($103.4 billion) net loss on revenue of US$16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026, versus a US$13 billion net loss on revenue of US$1.2 billion in the same period last year, the filing showed.

The company has mainly focused on serving the enterprise market. Anthropic’s net revenue retention, a measure of its ability to keep its existing customers and increase their spending over time, is about 900%, the filing showed.

See also: Sembcorp gauges demand for US$394 mil India unit IPO — Bloomberg

Anthropic said 79% of its revenue came from customers outside of its top five customers for the third quarter of the year.

Anthropic is seeking to tap the public market’s ample funding capacity to maintain its lead over rivals, as AI companies burn through hundreds of billions of dollars to continue advancing their so-called frontier models.

See also: Mi Material to be spun off from Bursa-listed parent; bets on China+1 for growth

It is set to begin formally marketing for its IPO as soon as the week of Nov 9, Bloomberg News has reported. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s record-setting IPO, people familiar with the matter have said.

The company and its rival OpenAI are also facing mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, ramping up concern about the potential impact on Anthropic’s market debut.

Anthropic emphasised the potential for its AI to “behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” in the filing. If its technologies are not developed with adequate safeguards and oversight, it could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy”.

Consumption-based revenue rose from US$288 million, and 75% of the company’s revenue, for the year that ended Dec 31, 2024 to US$3.8 billion, and 83% of the total, for last year. Information technology made up US$13.1 billion, and 80% of revenue, between January and June of this year. For Anthropic, consumption-based revenue refers to customers that pay for its AI models as they use them, based on the amount of tokens and the type of AI model they use.

The company’s total indebtedness stood at US$6.2 billion as of June 30, and it said it could raise more debt going forward to meet its financing needs.

Anthropic said it has a revolving credit facility of up US$15 billion, which it increased in size from US$3.25 billion. Revolving loans work much like a credit card, allowing a company to borrow, repay and borrow again up to a set limit over the life of the facility. They are commonly used by companies to provide financial flexibility and ready access to liquidity when needed. The revolver will mature in 2031, the company said.

It added that, after obtaining an investment-grade credit rating from at least two of the three major credit rating agencies, the revolving loan could become unsecured.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The company spent US$8.9 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the six months that ended June 30, up 283% from the year prior. The company noted that these expenses declined as a percentage of revenue, seemingly responding to concerns about the pace of spending.

Just since the end of 2025, Anthropic entered into new agreements for computing power with minimum obligations of about US$417 billion. These agreements will generally start this year or next, with terms as long as 20 years.

Anthropic’s compute economics have improved as revenue has scaled. Compute and infrastructure spending was more than 10 times revenue in 2023, falling to 653% in 2024, 160% in 2025 and just 55% in the first half of 2026. In the second quarter alone, it fell further to 48% of revenue — meaning Anthropic was spending about 48 cents on compute and infrastructure for every dollar of sales.

Goldman Sachs touted its role in the coveted lead-left position in marketing documents sent to clients, after securing the same role for the record-setting listing of SpaceX earlier this year, a document seen by Bloomberg showed. Morgan Stanley, its rival, is the so-called stabilisation agent, a sought-after role that would see it engage in transactions that reduce volatility in the stock, the filing showed.

title: EQT to buy Range Resources, creating largest US gas producer
article:
(Oct 26): EQT Corp agreed to buy Range Resources Corp in an all-stock deal for about US$12.8 billion, creating what it says will be the largest and only vertically integrated US natural gas producer.

The merged company will pump more than nine billion cubic feet equivalent of daily production in Appalachia, where both companies are big operators. It will hold over 30 years of drilling inventory across nearly three million net acres. EQT expects US$325 million in annual savings within two years.

EQT chief executive officer Toby Rice is pushing to build a US gas giant with the scale to sell directly to LNG markets and power plants. A self-styled “shalennial,” Rice took control of the company in 2019 after a proxy fight. He has turned the driller into an integrated producer, adding assets across the region and re-merging with a pipeline operator in 2024.

The deal also comes as US natural gas production continues to grow, outpacing the increase in oil output. Gas has emerged as a key energy source to generate power for the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. EQT and Range’s combined assets are adjacent to Data Center Alley, a part of Northern Virginia that has become a popular location for data centres.

“This transaction comes at a pivotal moment for America’s economy, as a convergence of modern industry and energy ushers in a new era of growth,” Rice said on a call with analysts on Monday. “Nowhere is this transformation more evident than in Appalachia.”

Shares of Range Resources climbed 9.4% to US$49.86 at 8.33am in New York in pre-market trading. EQT shares were down 8.4%.

Range shareholders will receive 0.987 EQT shares for each share held and will own about 27% of the combined company, according to a statement. EQT is paying a takeover premium of about 20% to Range’s closing share price last Friday, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Vincent Piazza.

The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. Citigroup Inc and RBC Capital Markets LLC are financial advisers to EQT. Kirkland & Ellis LLP is EQT’s legal counsel. Evercore Inc is lead financial adviser to Range and JP Morgan Securities LLC also advised the company, while Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP is its legal counsel on the deal.

title: SpaceX agrees to US$40 bil chip-financing deal with Apollo
article:
(Oct 26): SpaceX signed a roughly US$40 billion ($51.25 billion) equipment-finance lease with Apollo Global Management Inc to pay for the chips needed to fuel its artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions.

The fixed-rate that the company will pay will be determined at pricing, which hasn’t yet occurred, SpaceX said in a filing on Monday. The deal is expected to close before year end, and the leases are expected to start in the first half of next year.

Elon Musk touted the deal to help finance purchases of Nvidia Corp’s graphics processing units in a post on X over the weekend.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX said in a statement on Monday, adding that it’s seeing “less than one year payback periods” on its AI investments.

The agreement comes on the heels of a tumultuous week for AI companies in debt markets as concern mounted over the industry’s rapid spending, and limited profits so far to show for it. With investors demanding increasingly large premiums to finance the AI build-out, the volatility roiled pricing discussions over the SpaceX debt, which is being structured as private bonds to be issued by an off-balance sheet entity.

Much of the investor angst has been focused on the so-called neoclouds, which sell high-end computing power to technology companies. Musk has sought to differentiate his company from those businesses, pointing to SpaceX’s revenue from its Starlink business and rocket launches.

See also: Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul

SpaceX, which is rated investment-grade by the three largest credit graders, has seen the price of its own debt tumble in recent weeks. Credit-default swaps tied to the company, which are used to insure against losses on its debt, surged last week to a record 266 basis points at the close of trading last Friday, a level more typical of a junk-rated borrower. That concern eased slightly in early trading on Monday, with SpaceX swaps trading around 261 basis points, ICE Data Services prices showed.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc served as the sole structuring agent on the deal, according to the statement. Funds and accounts managed by BlackRock Inc, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and capital accounts advised by KKR & Co also made anchor commitments.

title: PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime
article:
(Oct 26): Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wants the UK to rejoin the European Union (EU) during his lifetime, calling for an “honest” discussion about the impact of Brexit.

“I don’t think things have worked out as people said they would,” Burnham told ITV of his country’s 2016 decision to leave the bloc, adding that he wasn’t proposing any changes during this Parliament. “I’m going to lead a discussion on how we make it better.”

Reshaping Britain’s relationship with the European Union has become one of Burnham’s key pledges since he became the prime minister three months ago, as he gambles on revisiting a divisive issue that dominated UK politics over the last decade. The 56-year-old prime minister opened the door to rejoining the EU at his party’s annual conference last month, saying he would set out options for a new relationship later this year.

Burnham said he wouldn’t seek to re-run the 2016 referendum, nor break Labour’s 2024 election pledge not to join the EU’s single market or customs union.

He was speaking ahead of a UK-EU summit which is due to take place on Nov 20, when the prime minister has said he wants to make progress on boosting economic growth and tackling illegal immigration into the UK.

See also: Axel Springer to cut Telegraph jobs after buying UK newspaper

Burnham said he’s seeking a deal that aims “to support our farmers, our food manufacturers, but also to increase collaboration on immigration because we lost that and we need to get it back”, he told Sky News later on Monday. “I’m talking about practical steps to deal with the things that matter to people.”

He said the UK had stronger return agreements for the arrival of people in small boats when it was in the EU, and that immigrants have now become more likely to settle in the country permanently, rather than leaving after a few years.

He added that he will “never move ahead” of public opinion on the issue of Brexit, though it’s unclear how he intends to achieve that. Asked whether Burnham would use a referendum or a general election to gain a mandate for his new EU position, his deputy official spokeswoman Cat Simmons declined to comment.

See also: UK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil

“We’re not at that stage yet,” Simmons said to reporters at a briefing on Monday. “The first step here is the substance rather than the process.”

Burnham also used the ITV interview to rule out an early election, saying it’s not something he’s thinking about.

“There is no election coming any time soon,” he said. “Britain is starting to regain its momentum.”

title: Soybeans hit two-month low as Lula’s win lifts China trade outlook
article:
(Oct 26): Soybean futures fell to a two-month low in Chicago, while coffee and sugar slumped as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise election win in Brazil hit the nation’s currency, boosting export prospects for the commodity powerhouse.

 

Lula won a fourth term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a political upset that comes as a setback to investors who had backed his rival to rein in the country’s deficit. Brazilian markets are heading for a rout when local trading begins with a currency derivatives contract on the CME exchange showing the real at 5.60 a dollar, which implies a 12% plunge from Friday’s close. Trading on the real opens at 8am New York time.

A weaker real boosts the competitiveness of Brazilian produce, encouraging exports as farmers receive more local currency for their crops. As Brazil is the world’s biggest exporter of sugar, coffee and soy, that’s bearish for prices.

 

The most-actively traded soybean contract on the Chicago Board of Trade dropped as much as 1.7% to the lowest since late August. Lula’s emphasis on pragmatic engagement with China could further entrench Brazil’s dominance as the Asian nation’s top soybean supplier and erode the US’s share of the world’s biggest soybean import market.

Brazil has increasingly taken more market share in China, accounting for nearly 80% of its imports in the first nine months of the year, despite Beijing’s trade deal with the US, its No 2 supplier. At the same time, China has boosted investment in the South American country’s port infrastructure, including terminals at Santos built by top crop trader Cofco Corp.

“Lula is pro exports of beans to China, so that is bearish US soybeans if Brazil can fulfill more of China’s needs,” said Joe Davis, director of commodity sales at Futures International LLC.

The weakness spilled over into edible oils, with soyoil futures dropping as much as 1.2% in Chicago and palm oil falling as much as 1.1% in Kuala Lumpur, snapping a two-day advance. Palm oil typically tracks soyoil because they compete for many of the same food and biofuel markets.

See also: Copper slumps as surging stocks and tech-stock selloff sour mood

Elevated Malaysian inventories also weighed on the market despite an improvement in export demand, according to Tasvinderjit Singh, director and head of futures at CGS International Futures Malaysia.

Sugar and coffee futures also dropped when trading opened on Monday. The most-actively traded sugar contract fell as much as 3.6%, the most in over a month, while arabica coffee dropped as much as 3.3%. Robusta fell to a two-year low.

The move is a “simple technical reaction” to the expected currency move, according to Arnaud Lorioz, chief executive officer of Paris-based brokerage Deepcore. “The market is saying the real will favour more exports from sugar producers in Brazil.”

See also: Nickel rallies past US$16,000 on prospect of Indonesia output cuts

Lula’s re-election brings his nation’s relationship with the US into question, given his ideological differences with President Donald Trump. In July, the US president hit Brazil with a 25% tariff, but Trump has also praised Lula’s intelligence and found him to be a “good man”.

The way the relationship between the two leaders develops could have longer-term impacts on agricultural markets, said Carlos Mera, head of agricultural commodities research at Rabobank. “The US can impose a number of measures on countries that they see as enemies,” he added.
• Soybeans dropped 1.4% to US$12.53 a bushel as of 10.20am in London
• Raw sugar was 2.3% lower in New York

title: TeleChoice wins new $1.3 bil contract from U Mobile
article:
TeleChoice International has won a new contract worth up to $1.3 billion from its key customer U Mobile to provide logistics services, thereby contributing positively to its earnings from FY2027 onwards.

​The new contract, which will take place after the existing one expires next February, is confirmed for the first three years with the option to extend for another two years.

"This renewal is a strong vote of confidence in us, and we are grateful for the partnership. In just three years, the network we manage for U Mobile has grown from over 600 to more than 1,000 touchpoints across Malaysia," says Pauline Wong, president and CEO of TeleChoice.

"As U Mobile extends the nationwide reach of its ULTRA5G network, we will invest further in our people, systems and automation. We will also build on this experience to take our managed services business further across the region,” she adds.

Wong Heang Tuck, CEO of U Mobile, says this renewed agreement with TeleChoice builds on the operational capabilities the two teams have developed together.

"It will help us respond to changing demand across our sales and distribution channels as we expand our 5G network nationwide. This supports our vision of being Malaysia’s preferred mobile and digital services provider," he adds.

See also: Vodafone boosts cost-cutting target for UK to £1 bil by 2032

TeleChoice International last traded at 20 cents. It is up 16.47% year to date.

title: Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul
article:
(Oct 26): The Dutch government aims to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive targeting annual savings of €3.5 billion (RM16.01 billion).

The central government wants to save €900 million a year by 2027, rising to €3.5 billion from 2035. That amounts to around 25,000 jobs, spread over several years, according to a government statement on Monday. The cabinet will present plans for deploying artificial intelligence to work more productively early next year.

“We cannot keep doing what we have been doing,” State Secretary for Effective Government Eric van den Burg said. “That is why we are going to make tough choices for a central government that really works: simpler, smarter, and smaller.”

The number of government officials surged to a record 160,000 at the end of 2025, up 41% compared to 2018, despite pledges by previous cabinets to scale back headcount.

The Dutch government budget deficit of 1.8% is one of the smallest in the European Union. Yet the figure and its long-term outlook still raise concerns in the Netherlands, which has a reputation for being fiscally conservative.

The cuts won’t hit equally hard everywhere, with police and defence among exempted areas.

See also: Meta seeks up to US$95 bil in equity to fund AI spending

Ministries, inspectorates and implementing agencies will be most impacted, according to a letter Van den Burg sent to parliament. Departments there could face “significant staffing implications” of reductions of 45% or even 60%.

Van den Burg emphasised that the reductions go hand-in-hand with government ambitions to cut red tape. Its flagship programme to scrap 500 unnecessary or overly bureaucratic rules per year should make the organisation “fundamentally more simple” and lessen the need for more staff.

Promising technological developments are also paving the way for fewer external hires and a smaller administration. Various AI initiatives have already been launched in recent years across different parts of the government and the goal is to “apply AI even more broadly” to increase productivity, Van den Burg says.

See also: SK Hynix shares defy AI sell-off with help from Kioxia gains

He cited a string of non-binding motions passed by parliament calling on the cabinet to increase government productivity by 20% through AI as a reason for the cuts. He also said that the push aims to work as much as possible with Dutch and European suppliers to avoid getting dependent on non-European technology.

title: Meta seeks up to US$95 bil in equity to fund AI spending
article:
(Oct 26): Meta Platforms Inc is seeking to raise as much as US$95 billion from selling common and preferred stock, tapping investors for support in the race to lead artificial intelligence’s development.

The company is offering about US$35 billion of common and preferred stock, according to a statement Monday. It will also raise about US$60 billion in an at-the-market share sale programme, which allows companies to sell shares in the open market from time to time. The ATM will consist of its planned Class C non-voting shares.

Meta’s shares pared initial losses to trade up 1.2% at US$650 each in pre-market trading on Monday in New York. Its shares have fallen 2.7% this year through Friday’s close.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg overhauled the company’s AI operation through an aggressive hiring push and has launched new products as well as committed hundreds of billions of dollars to build out the infrastructure needed to support the models.

The company has unveiled a personal AI agent known as Muse and an AI model called Muse Wonder that leadership say is on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude in terms of tasks such as coding.
